screens.title: Creating user accounts with useradd
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a user account is more than giving a name. The useradd utility creates the account record and, with the right options, prepares the user environment. A common workflow is to use -m to create the home directory so the user has a place for configuration files, -s to set a login shell like /bin/bash, -c to include a comment such as a full name or department, and -g to assign an existing primary group. If -g is omitted many systems create a private group with the same name as the user. For example, a practical command is: sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -c "Jane Doe" -g developers jane. doe. After creation, you must set a password with sudo passwd jane. doe. One misconception is assuming useradd sets a usable shell and home by default on every distribution — defaults vary, so be explicit in scripts. Another trap is creating the user without a primary group, which can lead to unexpected file permission behavior. Practice creating accounts with explicit options, then verify with id and by listing the home directory to confirm ownership and permissions. Reflect: what default behavior would cause a new user to be unable to write to their home directory?

keyIdea.title: Create with intent
keyIdea.text: Use -m, -s, -c and -g to ensure a new account is provisioned with a home, shell, identity, and proper primary group.

content.html:
Core Concept

useradd usage and examples

Create a user with options to ensure a home directory, default shell, comment, and primary group for predictable permissions.

Command example
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -c "Jane Doe" -g developers jane.doe
sudo passwd jane.doe
Common mistake
Omitting -m leaves no home directory; omitting -g can create an unexpected private group. Verify with id and ls -ld /home/username.
Pro tip
Make scripts explicit about shell and group choices so provisioning is predictable across systems.
What to verify
  • id jane.doe shows UID, primary group, and supplementary groups.
  • ls -ld /home/jane.doe confirms ownership and permissions.
  • cat /etc/passwd | grep jane.doe shows the shell and home path fields.
Key Takeaway

Always create accounts with the options required for immediate use and run verification commands to confirm correct setup.

screens.title: UIDs, GIDs, Primary and Supplementary Groups
screens.narratorSegment: Every user and group on a Linux system is represented by a numeric identifier. A UID is the unique number assigned to a user record; the OS uses it internally when enforcing file ownership and access control. Similarly, a GID identifies a group. When a user is created, they are assigned a primary group, which typically controls default file group ownership for new files. They can also belong to supplementary groups that grant access to shared resources without changing the primary group. For instance, a developer might have a primary group named after their username but be a member of a developers group as a supplementary group to access project files. A common misconception is thinking group names are enforced at login; the kernel uses numeric IDs, so renaming a group does not change ownership if you don’t update memberships. To inspect numeric IDs and memberships, use id username and check /etc/passwd and /etc/group. Understanding numeric IDs is crucial when moving files between systems or restoring from backups, because mismatched UIDs or GIDs can make files appear to belong to the wrong user. Consider this when migrating home directories or when a user’s name is changed.

keyIdea.title: Identifiers control ownership
keyIdea.text: UIDs and GIDs are the kernel’s truth. Names are conveniences; numeric IDs determine file ownership and permissions.

content.html:
Definition

UIDs and GIDs explained

Numeric identifiers are how the kernel tracks ownership. Names map to IDs in configuration files but are secondary to the kernel’s view.

Primary group
Controls default group ownership of new files; assigned at account creation and recorded as GID in /etc/passwd.
Supplementary groups
Grant additional permissions across shared resources, added using usermod -aG.
Inspecting IDs
id alice
# sample output: uid=1001(alice) gid=1001(alice) groups=1001(alice),1002(developers)
Analogy
Think of UIDs/GIDs like employee ID numbers. A name may change but the ID is how payroll and access systems recognize the person.
Common mistake
Assuming renaming a group updates ownership on disk; ownership follows numeric IDs, so ensure GIDs and memberships are consistent when migrating data.
Key Takeaway
Always verify numeric IDs when moving files between systems to avoid access surprises.

screens.title: Modifying accounts with usermod
screens.narratorSegment: usermod is the tool to change existing accounts without recreating them. You can change a user's login name, their login shell, home directory, and add supplementary groups. For example, to add a user to multiple supplementary groups you’d use sudo usermod -aG sales,marketing jane. doe. The -a with -G is essential: omitting -a replaces the user's supplementary groups rather than adding to them, which is a frequent and harmful mistake because it silently removes existing memberships. To change the default shell use sudo usermod -s /bin/zsh username, and to move or rename a home directory use -d with -m to move files: sudo usermod -d /home/newdir -m username. Renaming a user employs -l, but be careful: renaming does not automatically update file ownerships unless you correct UIDs or adjust file ownership. Always verify changes with id, grep in /etc/passwd, and ls on home directories after running usermod. When scripting, add checks to confirm that groups exist before assigning them and that the -a flag is used so you don’t accidentally strip access from a user. Modifying accounts with usermod means when adding supplementary groups, always use -ag to append groups; otherwise you overwrite existing memberships.. In practical terms, change shell, home directory, username, and add supplementary groups. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Use -a with -G
keyIdea.text: When adding supplementary groups, always use -aG to append groups; otherwise you overwrite existing memberships.

content.html:
Process Flow

Common usermod operations

  1. Append to supplementary groups: sudo usermod -aG sales,marketing jane.doe
  2. Change login shell: sudo usermod -s /bin/zsh jane.doe
  3. Move home directory: sudo usermod -d /home/newdir -m jane.doe
  4. Rename account: sudo usermod -l newname oldname
Pitfall
user﻿mod -G list without -a replaces memberships. That can remove access unexpectedly.
Example
sudo usermod -aG developers,git bob
sudo usermod -s /bin/bash bob
sudo usermod -d /home/bob_new -m bob
Verify
Run id bob and grep bob /etc/passwd to confirm shell and home directory changes.
Key Takeaway
Use usermod for safe in-place changes and always verify the result to avoid accidental loss of group memberships.

screens.title: Removing accounts with userdel
screens.narratorSegment: Removing an account is a sensitive operation because it can permanently delete a user’s files. The userdel command removes the account record. If you also want to remove the user’s home directory and mail spool, run sudo userdel -r username. Forgetting the -r option leaves behind the home directory and any owned files, which can become orphaned data and expose sensitive information. A useful approach is to archive the user’s home directory first, verify the archive, and only then delete. For example, create a tarball of /home/olddev, move it to an archive location, and then sudo userdel -r olddev. Another misconception is thinking supplementary group entries must be manually removed: when a user is deleted, they are automatically removed from supplementary groups. However, if the deleted user was the primary owner of shared resources, review permissions and reassign ownership as needed. Always verify deletion with grep username /etc/passwd and check for lingering files with find / -uid UID. If you need to preserve files but prevent login, consider locking the account first with passwd -l or changing the shell to /sbin/nologin before deletion.

keyIdea.title: Delete carefully
keyIdea.text: Use userdel -r to remove user data when appropriate, but archive first and verify no critical files will be orphaned.

content.html:
Process Flow

Safely removing a user account

  1. Archive files: sudo tar -czf /var/archives/olddev-home.tgz /home/olddev
  2. Verify archive integrity and move to secure storage.
  3. Delete account and home: sudo userdel -r olddev
  4. Confirm removal: grep olddev /etc/passwd and find / -uid UID
Common mistake
Running userdel without -r leaves homes and mail spools, which can contain sensitive data and waste disk space.
Alternative: disable first
If unsure, lock the account with sudo passwd -l username or set shell to /sbin/nologin until you confirm data preservation policies.
Key Takeaway

Always archive and verify before deleting accounts and use userdel -r when you intend to remove the home and mail spool.

screens.title: Group management: groupadd, groupmod, groupdel
screens.narratorSegment: Groups simplify permission management by bundling users who need the same access. Use groupadd to create a new group, for example sudo groupadd project_alpha. To rename a group or change its numeric GID, use groupmod; renaming is done with sudo groupmod -n project_beta project_alpha. When removing a group with groupdel, ensure it is not the primary group for any user — otherwise you may leave users with invalid primary group references; change their primary group first if needed. Group membership is typically managed by adding users to supplementary groups with usermod -aG. A misconception is thinking groups only affect file permissions; they also serve as a convenient way to grant sudo privileges when combined with sudoers entries. Always verify group membership with grep groupname /etc/group and id username. Before deleting a group, search for files owned by that GID so you can reassign ownership as necessary. Group management keeps your access model scalable: instead of granting permissions to individuals, grant them to a group and manage membership centrally. Group management: groupadd, groupmod, groupdel means use groups to grant shared permissions; manage membership centrally and verify before renaming or deleting groups.. In practical terms, organizing users for shared permissions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition

Group management commands

  • sudo groupadd project_alpha — create a new group
  • sudo groupmod -n project_beta project_alpha — rename a group
  • sudo groupdel project_beta — remove a group after verifying members
Example
Create a developers group, add bob: sudo groupadd developers; sudo usermod -aG developers bob; verify with grep developers /etc/group.
Checklist before delete
Confirm no user has the group as primary, reassign ownership of files with find and chown if needed, then groupdel.
Key Takeaway

Groups scale access management: change group membership to change access for many users at once.

screens.title: Password management and policies
screens.narratorSegment: Passwords are the first line of defense for interactive accounts, so setting and enforcing strong password rules is essential. Use passwd username to set an initial password; the command prompts for the new password and confirmation. Strong policies are enforced using PAM modules such as pam_pwquality. Administrators typically configure minimum length, required character classes, and denial of commonly used passwords. A misconception is assuming passwd alone enforces strength; without PAM rule configuration weak passwords may still be accepted. Also, password hashes live in /etc/shadow which is readable only by root; this prevents casual disclosure of hashed secrets. When creating accounts in bulk, provision strong temporary passwords and force a password change on first login by setting the password expiry or using chage. Be mindful of automation: scripts that set passwords must avoid logging plaintext secrets and should use secure vaulting when possible. Finally, consider account locking with passwd -l for compromised accounts and ensure you document recovery steps so legitimate users can regain access without exposing root credentials. Password management and policies means use passwd for setting passwords and pam configuration (pam_pwquality) to enforce strong, system-wide password rules.. In practical terms, setting passwords and enforcing strength with pam. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition

Password management essentials

Set initial passwords, require change on first login when needed, and enforce strength with pam_pwquality settings in PAM configuration files.

Commands
sudo passwd bob
# lock an account
sudo passwd -l compromised_user
# force change on first login
sudo chage -d 0 newuser
Security note
Never transmit plaintext passwords in scripts or logs. Use vaulting for automation and force password change at first login.
Misconception
passwd does not enforce system policy by itself; PAM configuration determines allowed password complexity.
Key Takeaway

Enforce password strength via PAM and avoid insecure handling of plaintext passwords in automation.

screens.title: System files: /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group
screens.narratorSegment: Account and group metadata lives in a small set of critical files. /etc/passwd contains basic account fields: username, placeholder for password, UID, GID, comment, home directory, and default shell. Historically it contained password hashes, but for security those moved to /etc/shadow, which is readable only by root and stores encrypted password hashes and aging information. /etc/group lists groups with their GIDs and member names. While these files are human-readable and sometimes inspected directly, modifying them by hand is risky because a syntax error can break login or group resolution. Use useradd/usermod/userdel and groupadd/groupmod/groupdel to update them safely — these utilities maintain consistent formatting. For troubleshooting you can view entries with cat or grep, for example cat /etc/passwd | grep bob, but always prefer commands for changes. If you must edit, use vipw or vigr which perform locking and validation. Understanding the structure of these files helps when recovering accounts or investigating permission issues, but keep edits through the proper tools whenever possible. screens.title: Configuring sudo with visudo and the wheel group
screens.narratorSegment: Granting sudo access lets administrators delegate specific or broad privileges without sharing the root password. The safest way to edit the sudoers configuration is visudo; it locks the file and checks syntax before saving, preventing accidental lockouts. A common pattern on RHEL is to add an admin user to the wheel group and enable wheel in sudoers with a line such as %wheel ALL=(ALL) ALL. For passwordless sudo you would use %wheel ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL. These entries allow group-based delegation: add a user to wheel with sudo usermod -aG wheel username and they gain the configured privileges. Misconfigurations are common: a syntax error in sudoers can block sudo for all users, and granting NOPASSWD: ALL is risky because it removes an important audit and deterrent. Prefer granting only the commands necessary for a role when possible. After changing sudoers, test by switching to the user and invoking a harmless privileged command such as sudo id or sudo ls /root to verify the expected permissions and behavior. Always follow the principle of least privilege when designing sudo policies. Configuring sudo with visudo and the wheel group means always edit sudoers with visudo and prefer group-based entries like wheel to manage admin privileges securely.. Definition

Sudo and visudo basics

Use visudo to edit /etc/sudoers safely. Grant rights with group entries to avoid editing many individual lines.

Common entries
# allow wheel group to run any command
%wheel ALL=(ALL) ALL
# allow wheel members to run any command without password
%wheel ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL
Example workflow
Add alice to wheel: sudo usermod -aG wheel alice. Edit sudoers with sudo visudo and verify with sudo -l as the user.
Misconception
Giving NOPASSWD: ALL is convenient but reduces accountability. Prefer least privilege and command-specific entries where possible.
Key Takeaway

Use visudo for safe edits and prefer group-based sudo entries to manage elevated privileges centrally.

screens.title: Onboarding: create alice (admin) and bob (developer)
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough demonstrates the full onboarding workflow from the chapter source. Start by creating the developers group if it doesn’t exist so you can assign bob to it. Then create alice with a home directory and bash shell, set her password, and add her to the wheel group so she can use sudo. Create bob, assign him to the developers group as his primary group and set his password. After each step run id username and grep for entries in /etc/passwd and /etc/group to confirm membership and settings. For example: sudo groupadd developers; sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -c "Alice Admin" alice; sudo passwd alice; sudo usermod -aG wheel alice; sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -c "Bob Developer" -g developers bob; sudo passwd bob; id alice; id bob; grep developers /etc/group. A common mistake is adding a user to a group without -a so supplementary groups are overwritten; here we use -aG when adding alice to wheel. After onboarding, validate that alice can sudo by switching users or running sudo -l and, if possible, performing a harmless privileged command such as sudo ls /root. This flow builds confidence in creating accounts and in verifying your changes.

Hands-on Activity

Onboard Alice and Bob

Execute these commands in sequence, then run verification commands to confirm state.

sudo groupadd developers

sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -c "Alice Admin" alice
sudo passwd alice
sudo usermod -aG wheel alice

sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -c "Bob Developer" -g developers bob
sudo passwd bob

id alice
id bob
grep developers /etc/group
Tips
Run commands with sudo and avoid scripting passwords in plain text. Use chage -d 0 to force initial password change if desired.
Common mistake
Omitting -a when adding groups removes existing memberships. Always append with -aG.
Key Takeaway

Provision accounts, set passwords, add necessary groups, and verify with id and /etc/group entries immediately.

Try this in your lab
Practice the sequence on a throwaway VM. After onboarding, test sudo by running sudo ls /root as alice. If sudo fails, check wheel membership and the sudoers file via visudo.

fullNarratorScript:
Managing users and groups is one of the most practical skills you’ll use every day as a Linux administrator. In this chapter you will learn how accounts are represented, how groups collect users for permission management, and how to grant elevated privileges safely. We’ll walk through the core tools: useradd, usermod, userdel for users; groupadd, groupmod, groupdel for groups; passwd for passwords; and visudo for sudo configuration. You’ll also learn which files store account and group metadata and why you should prefer the command-line utilities over manually editing system files. For example, creating a developer account with a home directory and assigning it to a project group is a routine task that prevents permission confusion later. You’ll practice onboarding two team members, confirm memberships with id and grep, and see common mistakes such as forgetting to remove a home directory when deleting accounts. By the end, you’ll understand the principle of least privilege and how groups and sudo let you follow it. Ready to explore each topic with commands, examples, and safety checks?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to create, modify, and remove user and group accounts cleanly and securely. You’ll learn the options that matter when running useradd, usermod, groupadd, and groupmod, and how those choices affect home directories, default shells, and primary groups. You will also manage passwords responsibly: setting initial passwords, enforcing stronger policy, and understanding why hashes live in a restricted file. Finally, you will configure sudo access without exposing the root password using visudo and group-based policies. Each objective maps to common administrator tasks: safely onboarding a new developer, giving an admin temporary elevated access, or fully removing a departing employee’s account. The narration and exercises emphasize safety checks, common mistakes, and verification commands so you gain practical confidence as well as conceptual clarity.

This second objectives slide highlights the practical tasks and files you will inspect directly. You will practice creating accounts with useradd using options such as -m to create a home directory, -s to set the default shell, -c to add a comment, and -g to select a primary group. You will modify accounts with usermod to change shells, home directories, usernames, and supplementary groups. You will remove accounts cleanly with userdel -r. You will also examine the canonical files that record accounts and groups: /etc/passwd for basic account metadata, /etc/shadow for password hashes restricted to root, and /etc/group for group membership. Finally, you will configure sudoers safely with visudo and test sudo for a new admin. These are not theoretical tasks: each maps to a verification command, such as id, grep, or cat, so you can confirm state after each change.

Creating a user account is more than giving a name. The useradd utility creates the account record and, with the right options, prepares the user environment. A common workflow is to use -m to create the home directory so the user has a place for configuration files, -s to set a login shell like /bin/bash, -c to include a comment such as a full name or department, and -g to assign an existing primary group. If -g is omitted many systems create a private group with the same name as the user. For example, a practical command is: sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -c "Jane Doe" -g developers jane. doe. After creation, you must set a password with sudo passwd jane. doe. One misconception is assuming useradd sets a usable shell and home by default on every distribution — defaults vary, so be explicit in scripts. Another trap is creating the user without a primary group, which can lead to unexpected file permission behavior. Practice creating accounts with explicit options, then verify with id and by listing the home directory to confirm ownership and permissions. Reflect: what default behavior would cause a new user to be unable to write to their home directory?

Every user and group on a Linux system is represented by a numeric identifier. A UID is the unique number assigned to a user record; the OS uses it internally when enforcing file ownership and access control. Similarly, a GID identifies a group. When a user is created, they are assigned a primary group, which typically controls default file group ownership for new files. They can also belong to supplementary groups that grant access to shared resources without changing the primary group. For instance, a developer might have a primary group named after their username but be a member of a developers group as a supplementary group to access project files. A common misconception is thinking group names are enforced at login; the kernel uses numeric IDs, so renaming a group does not change ownership if you don’t update memberships. To inspect numeric IDs and memberships, use id username and check /etc/passwd and /etc/group. Understanding numeric IDs is crucial when moving files between systems or restoring from backups, because mismatched UIDs or GIDs can make files appear to belong to the wrong user. Consider this when migrating home directories or when a user’s name is changed.

usermod is the tool to change existing accounts without recreating them. You can change a user's login name, their login shell, home directory, and add supplementary groups. For example, to add a user to multiple supplementary groups you’d use sudo usermod -aG sales,marketing jane. doe. The -a with -G is essential: omitting -a replaces the user's supplementary groups rather than adding to them, which is a frequent and harmful mistake because it silently removes existing memberships. To change the default shell use sudo usermod -s /bin/zsh username, and to move or rename a home directory use -d with -m to move files: sudo usermod -d /home/newdir -m username. Renaming a user employs -l, but be careful: renaming does not automatically update file ownerships unless you correct UIDs or adjust file ownership. Always verify changes with id, grep in /etc/passwd, and ls on home directories after running usermod. When scripting, add checks to confirm that groups exist before assigning them and that the -a flag is used so you don’t accidentally strip access from a user. Modifying accounts with usermod means when adding supplementary groups, always use -ag to append groups; otherwise you overwrite existing memberships.. In practical terms, change shell, home directory, username, and add supplementary groups. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Removing an account is a sensitive operation because it can permanently delete a user’s files. The userdel command removes the account record. If you also want to remove the user’s home directory and mail spool, run sudo userdel -r username. Forgetting the -r option leaves behind the home directory and any owned files, which can become orphaned data and expose sensitive information. A useful approach is to archive the user’s home directory first, verify the archive, and only then delete. For example, create a tarball of /home/olddev, move it to an archive location, and then sudo userdel -r olddev. Another misconception is thinking supplementary group entries must be manually removed: when a user is deleted, they are automatically removed from supplementary groups. However, if the deleted user was the primary owner of shared resources, review permissions and reassign ownership as needed. Always verify deletion with grep username /etc/passwd and check for lingering files with find / -uid UID. If you need to preserve files but prevent login, consider locking the account first with passwd -l or changing the shell to /sbin/nologin before deletion.

Groups simplify permission management by bundling users who need the same access. Use groupadd to create a new group, for example sudo groupadd project_alpha. To rename a group or change its numeric GID, use groupmod; renaming is done with sudo groupmod -n project_beta project_alpha. When removing a group with groupdel, ensure it is not the primary group for any user — otherwise you may leave users with invalid primary group references; change their primary group first if needed. Group membership is typically managed by adding users to supplementary groups with usermod -aG. A misconception is thinking groups only affect file permissions; they also serve as a convenient way to grant sudo privileges when combined with sudoers entries. Always verify group membership with grep groupname /etc/group and id username. Before deleting a group, search for files owned by that GID so you can reassign ownership as necessary. Group management keeps your access model scalable: instead of granting permissions to individuals, grant them to a group and manage membership centrally.
